useCases.title: Vesta Appliances: from impostors to Proof-of-Trust
useCases.summary:
Vesta Appliances is a fictional Swiss manufacturer with a very real problem: forty years of brand trust and no way to prove it online. Customers chat with fake support agents trading on Vesta's name, impostor technicians ring doorbells in Vesta livery, and nothing distinguishes the real services from the fakes.

The use case shows how Vesta becomes verifiable on the Verana Network, a public decentralized registry of registries. Its support chatbot and staff portal present ECS Service and Organization credentials as Linked Verifiable Presentations in their DID Documents, employees carry verifiable badges, repair partners hold Authorized Repairer accreditations issued under Vesta's own ecosystem governance. Anyone can resolve a Vesta service and see Proof-of-Trust before connecting: TRUSTED is earned from the credential chain, never just claimed.

It all runs live on the Verana testnet playground as an interactive story with runnable demos: verify the support chat from a personal wallet, check a technician's accreditation at the front door, and sign into the portal with a badge credential. Services are hosted by VS Agent, Verana's open-source business wallet.
useCases.userJourney:
Organization journey (Marc, CTO of Vesta): Marc deploys Vesta's Business Wallet (VS Agent) and anchors the company DID on the Verana Network. He completes KYB with an accredited issuer to obtain the ECS-Organization credential, then self-issues Service credentials so every Vesta service presents its identity as Linked VPs in its DID Document. He makes Vesta an ECS-Badge issuer for its ~200 employees and accredits a login service to verify those badges. Vesta's ISO 9001 certification becomes a verifiable credential, no re-certifying. Finally Marc builds the Vesta Repair Network, Vesta's own ecosystem with its own governance, issuing Authorized Repairer credentials that work at portal login and at the customer's front door.

User journey (runnable demos): choose a personal wallet, obtain an ECS-Badge from the demo issuer, log in to the staff portal as a repair employee with that badge instead of a password, then search the public directory of Authorized Repairers and check any repairer's Proof-of-Trust before opening the door.

useCases.title: Samsung SDS Unified Digital Wallet
useCases.summary:
Samsung SDS Unified Digital Wallet: Applying a Hierarchical Key Management Mechanism to Deliver Decentralized Identity, Security Token, and Stablecoin Services in a Single Digital Wallet

This use case designs an integrated key management structure that enables a financial holding company, together with its subsidiaries (bank, securities, capital, credit card company, etc.), to design and operate a wide range of services (STO, Stablecoin, DI, etc.).

Leveraging W3C DID/VC, the solution provides not only user eKYC/IAM but also a kill switch (ON/OFF) capability for policy functions, so that the wallet can respond flexibly to changes in the service provider's service policies.

It further provides functions covering digital wallet issuance requests, issuance, and personalization (PID, RBAC, Service Policy, etc.); service key management (STO key, Stablecoin key, blockchain address, Account key, etc.); and security/audit handling in the event of wallet loss or damage.

In particular, the Root Wallet can control the functions of Sub Wallets through a Policy function, newly applying a Master-Slave hierarchical function inheritance model.
useCases.userJourney:
(1) Membership Registration
- The user registers for the key custody service by submitting the required information with a PID (or vLEI for legal entities), which is used as a reference ID.

(2) Digital Wallet Provisioning
- A Master Wallet creates and assigns a Slave Wallet.
- After approval, the user's wallet, cryptographic keys, and Authentication VC are generated and issued.

(3) Wallet Activation
- The Authentication VC enables access to services within the integrated wallet.

(4) Service Usage
- KYC is performed through W3C DID/VC using the Authentication VC.
- For a new service (e.g., a Stablecoin wallet), the Authentication VC is presented for identity verification, and a Service VC is issued.
- After approval, the backend updates the user profile, and the service Master Wallet creates and assigns a Slave Wallet.
- During transactions, the Service VC is used as the primary credential for authorization. Additional VCs or approvals may be required.

(5) Wallet Update
- The user completes KYC, submits a change request with attestation, and receives a change code.
- After verifying the code and authorization, wallet information (e.g., cryptographic keys) is updated.

useCases.title: Reducing fraud, shrinking statewide expenses and driving digital identity value in California
useCases.summary: The California Community Colleges have been battling high volume attacks by fraudsters since 2018. These efforts were largely duplicative of the fraud fighting ecosystem at the California DMV, yet the systems lacked a point of integration to share data. When the California DMV made the digital identity stored in their mobile wallet available through the OpenCred platform, California Community Colleges rushed to adopt it. College bound students can now expedite their onboarding by verifying their identity upfront, providing assurance that their digital interactions are authentic. This expedites admissions, enrollment, and financial aid for students while also greatly reducing workload for college staff. The CCC Technology Center manages the OpenCred platform, now fully integrated with the statewide student account system, OpenCCC. In the first nine months, 160k individuals successfully verified their identity through the CCC/DMV integration, boosting the percentage of applicants who streamlined their journey via upfront identity verification by 12%.  Extending mDL to account recovery augmented this value, slashing administrative burden while protecting access for authentic students

organizations.labelRaw: California Department of Motor Vehicles (CA DMV)

useCases.userJourney: When a college bound student signs into, or creates their OpenCCC account, which is the first step in applying to a California Community College, they are prompted to verify their identity.  DMV mobile wallet is highlighted as the preferred option for anyone with a CA driver's license or ID card, and access to a smartphone.  New mDL users will download the app, scan their ID and do a selfie match.  mDL holders will only need to scan the QR code and accept the prompt to share information with the CCCs. Their OpenCCC account is then marked as verified, and they are prompted to continue with their application as a verified student. Colleges receiving the verified applications can then skip labor intensive local verification processes, and fastrack the student to enrollment/ financial aid.  OpenCCC users who lose access to their accounts can recover them using a similar mDL workflow: 1- scan the QR code, 2- accept data sharing, 3- confirm account details for a matched account, 4- gain access and reset their password.  5- use their verified account to submit a college admission application

useCases.title: Neoflow Digital Energy Passport for Cross-Border Crude Oil Clearance
useCases.summary:
Neoflow operates a digital rail for energy traceability across the Canada-U.S. border. Every batch of crude oil crossing by pipeline now carries a verifiable Digital Passport built with a set of W3C verifiable credentials proving, in real time, who owns it, where it came from, what it is, and where it sits.  

Today, a single batch of crude oil passes through 100-plus documents and 15-plus parties before clearing customs and it takes 45-90 days to do so, after the barrels have crossed the border. Furthermore, Importers who cannot prove USMCA origin may face tariffs.  

Neoflow solves this by issuing and consolidating W3C verifiable credentials at the batch level across its lifecycle, built on open VCDM and DID standards. Companies issue their own data, Neoflow holds and presents it, CBP verifies. Every credential is cryptographically signed, so origin clears digitally and cuts tariff exposure. 

Neoflow is life since July 2nd, 2026 and accounting for close to 25% of all oil flows from Canada into the US allowing crude oil importers to seamlessly share information about their products with US Customs and Border Protection.

credentials.labelRaw: Crude Oil Product Verifiable Credential (Digital Passport)

organizations.labelRaw: Canada’s largest crude oil importers (25% of the whole market)

useCases.userJourney:
Neoflow gives each company in a cross-border energy shipment an agent to create assertions about oil shipments as verifiable credentials. As a shipment moves from origin to a US destination, each party contributes the facts it is responsible for. Neoflow turns these into credentials and assembles one Digital Passport per shipment, which CBP and stakeholders can check instead of waiting on paper.

Companies are the data source, so they issue credentials for their part. Neoflow holds and presents them on their behalf, and CBP verifies them. Each credential is cryptographically signed, and parties see only what is relevant to their role.

1. Onboarding: A company joins once and registers identifying details as reusable credentials.
2. Before arrival: Parties contribute data; Neoflow assembles the Passport and presents it to CBP before crossing for early visibility.
3. In-transit and delivery: As the shipment moves and changes hands, each party adds its part and Neoflow updates the Passport in real time.
4. Entry and clearance: The customs broker files the entry and links it on Neoflow. With origin and movement already proven, clearance is faster and no separate USMCA proof is needed.

useCases.title: End-to-End Digital Business Workflows: Transforming KYB-KYC-KYS via EU Business Wallet
useCases.summary:
Use Case: This end-to-end digital business workflow automates and secures high-assurance onboarding across the business lifecycle
- Know Your Business (KYB): Foundation for obtaining the EBWOID and EUCC.
- Know Your Customer (KYC): Financial-sector onboarding, including IBAN issuance.
- Know Your Supplier (KYS): Supplier onboarding, including invoice submission.

Problem: Manual corporate verification is slow, costly, and creates friction. Gathering complex corporate data to comply with EU 
regulations (AMLR, GwG, e-invoicing, etc.), conducting periodic reviews, and preventing invoice fraud are key pain points.

Value: Dramatically reduces onboarding time and administrative effort while mitigating transaction risks. Issued once, reused across the EU, and shared through different channels.

Organizations: Bundesanzeiger Verlag (Identity Issuer), Deutsche Bank (IBAN Issuer/Verifier), Bosch (Holder/KYS Verifier), SBB (Supplier Holder/Invoice Issuer) and legal representatives (EUDI Wallet/authorized signatories).

Wallets: EU Business Wallets (Procivis/Spherity) securely store EBWOID, EUCC, Company Info, IBAN, and other attestations using OpenID4VCI/VP and SD-JWT standards.
useCases.userJourney:
(1) KYB - Legal Entity Identification and info
- A Bosch Representative presents their personal PID via EUDI Wallet to Bundesanzeiger Business Wallet (Spherity).
- Bundesanzeiger Verlag issues EU Business Wallet Owner Identification Data (EBWOID) and EU Company Credential (EUCC) attestations directly to Bosch Business Wallet (Procivis).

(2) KYC & Financial Onboarding
- Bosch presents its attestation (EBWOID, EUCC) alongside multi-source attestations (Ownership, VAT, UBO, etc.) 
to the Deutsche Bank Business Wallet (Procivis) .
- The Ultimate Beneficial Owner's (UBO) identity is verified via their personal EUDI Wallet.
- The corporate account contract is created and signed (skipped by demo).
- Deutsche Bank issues an IBAN Owner (IBAN-OV) Attestation directly to the Bosch Business Wallet.

(3) KYS & Invoice Issuing
- The supplier, SBB presents its corporate credentials (EBWOID, EUCC, VAT, etc.) for instant, automated KYS onboarding at Bosch.
- Additionally, SBB’s commercial Payment Terms and bank-issued IBAN-OV attestations are presented to secure the payment triggering.
- SBB delivers the ordered parts and issues a cryptographically signed eInvoice  to the Bosch Business Wallet&

useCases.title: Republic of Verandia: citizen IDs, business IDs and legal representation on one open trust registry
useCases.summary: A fictional democracy runs its own digital identity as sovereign infrastructure: every component is open source and self-hosted by its institutions, with no vendor to depend on. The Civil Registry operates its own issuing service for an eIDAS-2-compatible Citizen ID, the Business Registry issues verifiable Business IDs and Proofs of Legal Representation, and the Republic itself governs who may issue and who may verify, on a neutral public trust registry that a state can equally self-host. Citizens hold their credentials in the wallet they choose, from an open roster of independent open-source wallets, so no single app is ever mandated. One scan signs them in to the Tax Buro or their bank; an unauthorized lender's over-asking request and a fake refund portal are both refused, with proof.
useCases.userJourney: The Republic anchors everything on a Verifiable Public Registry: an open, neutral registry of ecosystems, schemas and permissions that a state can equally self-host. The National Business Registry becomes an accredited issuer of Organization credentials, so proving a company's identity is a lookup, not paperwork. The National Civil Registry runs its own open-source issuing service and creates the Citizen ID ecosystem: it defines the eIDAS-2-inspired schema and holds the ISSUER permission, while relying parties like the Tax Buro and Meridian Bank must obtain VERIFIER permissions before wallets will share anything, the registry analog of eIDAS 2 relying-party registration. Citizens scan a QR and receive the Citizen ID in any wallet from the open roster, over AnonCreds/DIDComm or OpenID4VCI (SD-JWT VC). Companies attach Business IDs to self-hosted business wallets and publish services; representatives add a Proof of Legal Representation. Before anything is shared, the wallet trust-resolves the counterparty against the registry and renders a Proof-of-Trust. An unauthorized lender that over-asks and a fake refund portal both fail resolution and are refused, with proof.

useCases.title: CEXA: reusable KYC for exchanges and banks, with the original issuer paid on every reuse
useCases.summary:
Exchanges and banks run the same identity checks on the same customers, pay an IDV provider each time, and lose over half their sign-ups at the KYC wall. The Travel Rule adds a second redundancy: institutions must identify the counterparty behind every transfer, so each joins several directories and resubmits the same license.

The Crypto Exchange Association (demo) is a runnable answer built on Verana: a trust ecosystem founded by exchanges, open to the banks that serve them. It governs one reusable credential, CEXA-Kyc, on both sides: only accredited members may issue it, and only accredited members may ask a wallet for it. Asking for KYC data is a privileged, paid act. When a member accepts another member's credential, the protocol routes the reuse fee to the institution that paid for the original check: the KYC file becomes an asset, and the customer opens an account in about a minute. A second credential, CEXA-VerifiedCounterparty, published on each member's DID and free to verify, replaces N Travel Rule directory subscriptions with one membership.

The institutions are fictional. The infrastructure is not: run the full loop today with ten integrated open-source wallets.
useCases.userJourney:
1. The Association anchors its trust registry on Verana's Verifiable Public Registry: two schemas, a digest-anchored governance framework, and its fee schedule (fees are example values).

2. Members join through vetted, paid, renewable on-chain onboarding. Validated members receive their CEXA-VerifiedCounterparty credential. Members must already be Verifiable Services: the Association issues memberships, not identity.

3. The customer's first exchange runs one full IDV check, seals the evidence bundle into their wallet, digest-bound, and issues CEXA-Kyc for free.

4. On reuse, the wallet trust-resolves the requester and checks its VERIFIER accreditation before presenting. The verifier re-binds the person (passport NFC plus face match), receives the sealed evidence as its own CDD file, and pays the protocol-split fee: 0.90 to the original issuer, 0.10 to the Association. No phone home: the issuer never learns where the customer went

5. Travel Rule desks read the counterparty credential from the member's DID, free

6. Failures fail closed: a verifiable exchange outside the Association resolves TRUSTED and is still refused; a revoked credential dies at every member at the next check

useCases.title: Honduras: Billetera Electronica Nacional (BIEN) - 4 gob authorities issuing into one citizen-controlled wallet
useCases.summary:
Honduras launched BIEN, a self-sovereign digital identity wallet letting citizens hold and present official state credentials from their phone. Four authorities issue into one wallet: RNP (biometric national ID, DNIB) and INM (residence card for foreign residents) are the foundational trust anchors; DNVT (driving licence) and DPI/National Police (firearms permit) build on that root of trust.

Before BIEN, each document came from a different authority and could only be verified in person. The real challenge was legal standing and institutional acceptance, not digitization. Resolution No. 37,196 gave the DNIB legal equivalence to the physical ID, and institutions were instructed to accept wallet credentials within a week of launch. In month one, roughly 200,000 credentials were issued across RNP, INM, DNVT and DPI, reaching Hondurans at home and in the US.

Built on open standards (W3C Verifiable Credentials/DIDs, DIDComm v2, OIDC4VCI/VP, SD-JWT, ISO specs), BIEN stores credentials encrypted on-device, unlocked by face and password, and discloses only the fields a verifier needs. Any authority can verify offline via an encrypted 2D barcode, no internet required.

issuers.labelRaw: DNVT (Direccion Nacional de Vialidad y transporte)
DIGER (Direccion de Gestion por Resultados) - Trust Authority: ecosystem operator and programme implementer

CDER- Carnet de Extranjero Residente(INM, Person Identification Data, PID)
PCD (Permiso de Conducir Digital, PuB-EAA Public Attestation of Attributes)
PPA (Permiso de Portación de Armas, PuB-EAA Public Attestation of Attributes)

useCases.userJourney:
1. The citizen downloads BIEN free (Google Play/App Store) and registers a phone number and password.

2. They select their identity provider: RNP for Honduran nationals, INM for legal foreign residents.

3. They capture their face with the front camera. A liveness check runs first, then it's matched 1:1 against the issuing authority's own biometric record — the authority verifies the citizen, not the platform.

4. The credential is issued into the wallet in seconds as a W3C Verifiable Credential paired with a 2D barcode carrying the signature and a biometric reference, enabling fully offline verification.

5. Using that credential as proof of identity, DNVT (driving licence) and DPI/National Police (firearms permit) issue further credentials into the same wallet — no re-enrolment needed.

6. To present a credential, the citizen unlocks the wallet with face and password, then shares it offline (2D barcode, no network needed), remotely (online transactions), or by proximity (NFC/BLE).

7. The citizen sees which fields are requested and consents before sharing (selective disclosure); only needed data leaves the device. Digital and physical documents carry equal legal weight.

useCases.title: From Repeated Verification to Reusable Trust: Re-imagining the Real Estate Purchasing Journey
useCases.summary:
Interac Verified™ credential service is Canada's reusable digital credential network, enabling consumers to verify their identity once and securely reuse it across multiple interactions. The solution addresses common challenges in high-assurance industries such as real estate: repetitive identity checks, fraud risk, compliance burden, and poor user experiences.

In this first-to-market use case, Interac issues a high-assurance credential and enables users to securely store it in the Interac Verified™ app. 

FCT, a leading real estate technology provider, embeds credential verification directly into existing real estate workflows, accelerating adoption and minimizing implementation effort.

Homebuyers can securely share their credential with relying parties, including realtors, brokers, lenders, and lawyers. Consent-based sharing and selective disclosure ensure only the required information is shared.

The result is faster transactions, reduced fraud, improved privacy, and a better user experience. By replacing repeated verification with reusable trust, Interac and FCT are modernizing identity verification for one of Canada's most important financial transactions: purchasing a home.
useCases.userJourney:
Step 1: Download the Interac Verified™ App

The user receives a verification request from a relying party (e.g., realtor, broker, or lawyer) via email, SMS, or QR code. They download and register for the Interac Verified™ app, which supports secure passkey-based sign-in.

Step 2: Create a Verified Credential

The user creates an Interac Verified™ Credential by completing two verification steps: authenticating with a participating Canadian financial institution and verifying their identity using a selfie and government-issued ID. Once completed, their credential is issued and securely stored on their device.

Step 3: Share and Reuse

When requested, the user consents to share their credential with a relying party. Through selective disclosure, only the required information is shared. The credential remains on the user's device for future use, enabling fast, secure verification across multiple transactions. Verify once, reuse many times.

useCases.title: SSITIZENS — Verifiable social aid: how municipalities, merchants and citizens exchange trust with Wallets
useCases.summary:
Social aid programmes suffer from shared friction: citizens face paperwork to reach benefits they are entitled to, administrations run manual processes with limited traceability, and local merchants deal with heavy justification workflows to claim payments back.

SSITIZENS redesigns this circuit with decentralized identity, verifiable credentials, and tokenized aid governed by smart contracts. Vulnerable citizens receive a verifiable credential attesting their right to benefit, hold it in a mobile wallet, and spend the aid at accredited local merchants using tokens backed by real money. Merchants get automatic, auditable reimbursement in euros. Administrations gain full traceability of every public euro spent.

The pilot ran with the City Council of Córdoba, the Uno a Uno social association and local merchants, each operating with its own digital identity. Results: 98% redemption rate, 90% less administrative workload. Selected under NGI TrustChain and awarded the 2025 Alastria Blockchain Award for Best Decentralized Digital Identity Project.
useCases.userJourney:
1. Municipality issues the credential. The City Council, as trusted issuer, signs a verifiable credential attesting the citizen's eligibility and delivers it to the citizen's mobile wallet via OID4VCI.

2. Merchants join with a business identity. Each shop is accredited through its own business wallet and receives an organizational credential proving it is a valid party in the programme.

3. Aid is minted as tokenized funds. The administration issues programmable tokens backed one-to-one by the budget. Smart contracts govern roles, scope, expiration and redemption.

4. Citizen pays with a QR. At the point of sale, the citizen scans the merchant's QR. The wallet presents the credential (OID4VP) and the smart contract transfers tokens to the merchant. No card, no password.

5. AI validates the purchase. The merchant uploads the receipt; an LLM-based module checks that items fall within eligible categories, with no manual review.

6. Automatic reimbursement. The smart contract triggers reimbursement to the merchant's bank account in euros. The full trail is recorded on-chain for real-time auditing.

useCases.title: Digital Product Passport Applying the CIRPASS Structure and Danube Business Wallet
useCases.summary:
Textile, fashion, and various other manufacturers are using KSPTS (K4Security Passport Traceability System, k4-dpp.com), the flagship Digital Product Passport (DPP) platform of K4Security, to strengthen regulatory compliance and supply chain transparency. KSPTS has successfully completed a Proof of Concept (PoC) for the fashion brand Harlie-K, and has issued DPP samples and completed verification for a wide range of product categories across multiple companies.
Each product registered on the KSPTS platform has its standardized data — including raw material sourcing origin, material composition, Carbon Footprint (CFP), regulatory certification documents, and Lifecycle information — linked to a digital passport. This solution supports machine-readable, transparent regulatory compliance reporting, enabling companies to track the environmental impact and product information across their entire supply chain in real time. Through KSPTS, K4Security provides an optimal solution that allows companies in the European Union (EU) to proactively respond to the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR) and Digital Product Passport (DPP) mandatory requirements for sustainable products.
useCases.userJourney:
[Overall process]
① Onboarding (DID/Wallet) → ② Tier-specific VC issuance → ③ Attaching DPP·QR code → ④ Verification → ⑤ Consumer lookup

1. Onboarding
   - As a DPP Issuer, the required DID is pre-registered. When registering the wallet, UNTP VC signing is requested from the Wallet.

2. Role issuance
   - A server-side wallet is issued to the Actor, and a Role VC is issued.
   - Through the Role VC, access rights to non-public data can be proven.

3. UNTP VC (DPP) issuance
   - Based on the product's raw data and materials, a source verification VC is generated.
   - Based on the source verification VC, a UNTP DPP is issued.
   - The DPP is published via the product's DID Document.

4. DPP lookup
   - Data is accessed and verified through the product's DID.
   - When accessing linked non-public data (DCC or DTE, etc.) via the idr, authentication is performed.
   - Access rights are verified through submission of a RoleVC issued by ID/PW or REO.
   - Once access rights are confirmed, the non-public data can be viewed.

useCases.title: Credimi: Collaborative Automation for EUDI Interoperability and Conformance
useCases.summary:
Credimi is a shared automation and evidence platform for EUDI Wallet interoperability and conformance testing. It lets real wallets, issuers and verifiers from different countries and ecosystems be exercised in repeatable combinations, replacing bilateral demonstrations and manual testing with reusable workflows.

The platform automates both API interactions and end-user wallet journeys across physical or virtual devices. It captures structured results, protocol metadata, screenshots, video and device logs, then maps that evidence to a maintained source of truth covering EUDI ARF, OpenID, ETSI and regulatory requirements.

Credimi also translates Functional Conformance Assessment Framework (FCAF) test specifications into repeatable automated test journeys and reviewable evidence. Our implementation of the FCAF tests, will be presented at GDC 2026 on Day 2 at 14:00 in Room F.

The collaboration value is cumulative: each implementation added to the environment creates new interoperability combinations for the wider community. Developers, pilots, Member States and assessors can reproduce failures, compare behaviour, share findings and rerun the same tests after fixes.
useCases.userJourney:
Credimi integrates third-party interoperability and conformance services without making wallet developers rebuild automation for every provider. OpenID Foundation and WE BUILD test suites share one execution and evidence pipeline, while new services can be added through lightweight adapters.

1. A developer connects a device running the wallet, selects a test suite and chooses an issuance or presentation flow. No test-specific code needs to be added to the wallet application.
2. Credimi coordinates the external service, APIs and wallet actions. It drives QR-code or deep-link interactions across one or more devices and captures responses, metadata, screenshots, video, device logs and structured results. FCAF test results are extracted from these pipelines rather than produced by application-embedded test code.
3. The developer reviews the evidence, fixes the wallet and reruns the same journey. Results can be compared across releases and test suites.

Keeping the test logic in reusable automation pipelines cuts test implementation costs to a fraction of application-specific approaches and makes the automated tests reusable across wallets and assessment contexts.

useCases.title: Verifiable AI fairness: a seal for the system, a receipt for the person
useCases.summary: When an AI screens a job application, scores a loan or decides a benefit, the person affected gets a decision and no way to check whether it was fair. validant.ai issues two verifiable credentials that close that gap from both ends. The AI Fairness Seal is a credential whose subject is the AI system itself: a measurement engine cryptographically signs the fairness metrics, our server derives the verdict from those signed numbers, and the audited party never gets to assert its own result. The Decision Receipt is the person’s own credential, held in their wallet, naming which system decided, that it held a valid seal at the time, and optionally what would have had to change for a different outcome. The person presents it selectively to a third party, such as an ombudsman's office or a labor authority, revealing only what she chooses to reveal. Anyone can check a seal at validant.ai/verify without logging in or having an account. It runs on the same rails as the Swiss e-ID: SD-JWT VC, did:web and did:webvh, ES256, OpenID4VCI and OpenID4VP, with revocation on an IETF Token Status List.
useCases.userJourney:
1. An employer runs its CV-screening AI through validant.ai, self-service or commissioned, against a named, legally grounded fairness rule.
2. The engine computes and signs the metrics (Ed25519) with the CI method, multiplicity correction and minimum detectable effect.
3. validant.ai verifies the signature and derives the verdict itself; unsigned metrics are refused. A pass is earned, not claimed.
4. The Fairness Seal is issued as an SD-JWT VC (ES256, did:web:validant.ai): system, owner, LEI, metric, threshold, result, status pointer.
5. It arrives via OpenID4VCI in the employer's wallet; swiyu confirms the issuer.
6. The AI rejects Maria; the rejection email carries the seal as a scannable code.
7. She also gets a key-bound Decision Receipt in her swiyu wallet: which system decided, that its seal was valid, the decisive factors, and the smallest change that would have flipped it.
8. She presents it selectively over OpenID4VP to an ombuds office, which re-verifies the seal.
9. Anyone can verify a seal at validant.ai/verify, no login, in-browser, public key and status list.
10. If the assessment is invalidated, the seal is revoked and every check reads Revoked within seconds.

useCases.title: Cryptographically Verifiable Digital Product Passports for EU Battery Regulation Compliance
useCases.summary:
European manufacturers must issue Digital Product Passports (EU Battery Regulation
2023/1542, from 18 February 2027, with the ESPR extending this to further
categories). Today the data those passports need lives in unstructured PDF
datasheets, and manufacturers have no way to prove a downstream party has not
altered the file after publication.

AAS Studio turns a datasheet into a conformant Asset Administration Shell (IDTA,
IEC 63278-1:2023), then issues a W3C Verifiable Credential (VCDM 2.0, JWT-VC, and
an SD-JWT-VC variant with selective disclosure) committing to a canonical hash of
the passport content. The manufacturer is the issuer, signing with a tenant-scoped
ES256 key. Any verifier — regulator, recycler, supply-chain partner — checks the
credential against a public JWKS with no account and no call back to AAS Studio:
verification is fully offline. Revocation is enforced via a Bitstring/Token Status
List.
useCases.userJourney:
1. Manufacturer uploads a PDF datasheet; AAS Studio extracts the regulatory fields
   with an LLM ensemble and maps them onto a conformant Asset Administration Shell,
   validated against the official IDTA test engine.
2. AAS Studio computes a canonical hash of the passport content and issues a W3C
   Verifiable Credential signed with the manufacturer's own ES256 key, optionally
   as an SD-JWT-VC for selective disclosure.
3. If issued as revocable, a Bitstring/Token Status List slot is allocated; the
   manufacturer can revoke it later, effective immediately for any verifier.
4. The holder presents the credential's JWT to a relying party by any channel.
5. The relying party verifies it fully offline: it fetches the public JWKS and
   re-derives the proof itself, including the status-list check, so the verdict
   never depends on trusting AAS Studio's server.

useCases.title: CREDEBL: An Open-Source Digital Trust Infrastructure Enabling Trusted Digital Ecosystems
useCases.summary:
CREDEBL is an open-source Digital Public Good contributed by AYANWORKS under LFDT.

A. Bhutan NDI:

useCases.title: Trusted Caller Identity
useCases.summary:
Call centre authentication still relies on security questions and SMS OTPs, which can be stolen, spoofed or defeated by SIM swap. Customers must disclose personal data to agents who have no need to see it.

Trusted Caller Identity replaces this with a verifiable credential. Telefónica issues a credential proving phone number ownership, secured by its Number Verify and SIM Swap network APIs. When a customer calls, the contact centre opens an encrypted DIDComm channel to their wallet and the customer confirms biometrically on their own device. Selective disclosure returns only a yes/no answer, so no personal data reaches the agent. Verification time reduces >4 times.

Four organisations across telecoms, identity and standards built it: Telefónica Tech (issuer, network signals), Dock Labs/Truvera (credential infrastructure), TMT ID (identity data), GSMA (coordination). The customer holds the credential, the contact centre verifies it, and no party sits in the middle.

It uses open verifiable credential and DIDComm standards, and Telefónica's network APIs sit within GSMA Open Gateway, so the model can scale to any operator rather than stay proprietary. Demonstrated at M

Setup, once
1. Telefónica verifies the customer's number and device via its Number Verify and SIM Swap APIs, confirming control of the number and that no recent SIM change occurred.
2. It issues a verifiable credential proving phone number ownership.
3. The credential is delivered to the customer's wallet and stored on device, not in a central database. In production the wallet will sit inside the operator's existing app.

On the call
4. The customer calls; the agent or IVR triggers authentication.
5. The contact centre, as verifier, sends an encrypted DIDComm request straight to the customer's wallet.

Tampered, revoked and replayed presentations are rejected.

useCases.title: Reeco Textile DPP : the supply chain verified independently of the brand's systems
useCases.summary:
Textile passports today publish what a brand exports from its PLM. A signature makes that tamper-evident, not true. Reeco verifies the chain itself, from outside the brand's systems: every supplier lodges its documents directly with Reeco, and a proprietary mass balance, carrying the indices and the PEF calculation, bounds each claim to its certified evidence. No signed claim survives in excess of what the certificates cover.
The passport is issued from that result: a W3C Verifiable Credential from did:web:ia.reeco.eco, delivered over OpenID4VCI to an organisational or personal wallet, presented back over OpenID4VP and verified against the published DID document, eleven checks including holder key binding. Verification is the product; the passport is what verification leaves behind.

No textile DPP can be conforming yet: the delegated act is not adopted and service providers cannot register. This is a pilot, and says so. The stack is live and public.

useCases.title: Seal: independent review of AI decision evidence
useCases.summary:
A bank declines a loan application. Six months later, the customer's solicitor asks why. The only record of that decision is a log written by the organisation under review.

Seal addresses this by separating the evidence across three independent issuers: Seal signs the decision receipt, Yivi issues the reviewer's credential, and the reviewer signs the verdict. No single party controls the complete evidence path.

When a decision is questioned, a reviewer opens a docket with one fixed question, set before evidence is opened so it cannot be adjusted to fit the answer. Their browser verifies every signature, and they record one of three verdicts: accepted, declined or not enough to answer. Walk the flow and tamper with a receipt yourself: app.aqta.ai/demo.

What it establishes: Seal signed the stated record; signed fields have not changed; a reviewer holding a credential Aqta did not issue signed a verdict on a fixed question.

What it does not establish: that the record matches the computation that actually ran, or that every decision was recorded.

We would rather be checked than believed. The signing is production; this review flow is a prototype, and the page says so
useCases.userJourney:
1. An AI decision is signed by Seal at the moment it is made; the receipt is offline-verifiable against Seal's published Ed25519 key
2. An independent reviewer opens a docket: one fixed question, set before the evidence is opened so it cannot be adjusted to fit the answer, with the receipt attached. The question is hashed into what will be signed
3. The reviewer verifies the evidence in their own browser, then chooses one of three verdicts: accept, decline, or not enough to answer it
4. The page requests an IRMA signature session; the reviewer's Yivi wallet displays the exact binding text: receipt hash, question hash, decision, timestamp
5. The reviewer signs by disclosing a verified email credential from their wallet. No account is created with the relying party at any point
6. The relying party verifies the attribute-based signature using irmago, the open-source IRMA verification library, with the signing moment anchored by the Yivi timestamp service
7. The evidence pack exports: receipt, credential presentation, and countersignature. Each is independently verifiable without contacting Aqta

useCases.title: Decentralized PHC Credentials in the Future AI Era.
useCases.summary:
The primary motivation behind creating this proof of concept is to demonstrate how Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) and Verifiable Credentials (VCs), aligned with W3C standards, can be integrated with on-chain blockchain technology i.e (CHEQD). This approach enables the deployment, storage, and verification of proof of human identity.
What it does
1.Government ID Issuance: A government agency issues an ID to the holder, which is required to obtain a PHC Verifiable Credential (VC).

2.Presenting ID to PHC Provider: The holder presents their government-issued VC from their wallet to the PHC provider, a trusted authority.

3.Fingerprint Biometric Capture: Once the government ID is verified, the user scans their fingerprint using PHC’s biometric infrastructure, which extracts unique fingerprint features.

4.Online Authentication : When accessing an online service that requires PHC verification, the user shares the PHC credential from their wallet with the service.

5.Verification Process: The service provider’s DIDComm v2 agent performs ZKP verification with the holder’s data. If verified, access is granted; otherwise, it is denied.
useCases.userJourney:
The DIDComm v2 agent is implemented entirely in Python, enabling secure message exchange between the Issuer, Holder, and Verifier.
DID:Peer protocol implementation and DID generation are also developed in Python.
We use the Universal DID Resolver/Registrar with cheqd to register and resolve DIDs on the cheqd testnet.
The complete Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) circuit is written in Circom, with proofs generated using the Circom compiler.

Proof Generation Flow

Feature Extraction: Fingerprint bifurcation and termination points are extracted, flattened, and combined into a single array.

Poseidon Merkle Tree: The data is hashed into a Poseidon-based Merkle tree, producing the root commitment and 8 sibling hashes for efficient proof generation.

Proof Generation: The Circom circuit compiles using these hashes to generate the proof, verification key, and public inputs, which are signed by the issuer.

Verification: The verifier extracts the proof and public inputs from the credential and validates them using zk-SNARKs, returning true or false.

useCases.title: Verifiable Participant Identity for Cross-Border Financial Messaging

The trust challenge is ensuring that every institution communicating across the network is reliably identified and that all instructions are authenticated and tamper-evident. useCases.userJourney:

5. Verification: The receiving service validates the signature against the connection key, confirming the authenticated sender and intended recipient before processing.

useCases.title: Making the European Business Wallet real: EBW trial for national healthcare data exchange (KIK-V)

Organisation identification is issued as a qualified attestation (QEAA) aligned with emerging LPID/EBWOID formats, mandates prove who acts on behalf of the organisation, and employees sign in with their personal EUDI wallet. useCases.title: Direct e-Invoicing Small Scale Pilot
useCases.summary:

useCases.userJourney:

useCases.title: Transpareo - product truth anyone can verify
useCases.summary:

You are not trusting the brand, and you are not trusting us. You are checking the maths.

The impact is social: shoppers can tell real sustainability claims from marketing, repairers and recyclers get data they can trust, and regulators verify independently. useCases.userJourney:

useCases.title: Digital Certificate of Good Conduct (VOG) as a Verifiable Credential
useCases.summary:
Every year, 1.8 million Certificates of Good Conduct (VOGs) are issued in the Netherlands. Over 350 large organizations and 26,000 sports clubs rely on the VOG to screen employees, trainers and volunteers — but the paper/PDF process is slow (1–7 weeks), manual and vulnerable to fraud.

Justis, the screening authority of the Dutch Ministry of Justice and Security, is piloting the VOG as a verifiable credential together with Credenco. Citizens receive the VOG directly in their personal wallet; employers and clubs verify it instantly through the Credenco Business Wallet. Built on open standards (W3C Verifiable Credentials, EUDI Wallet ARF, DIIP v5) for interoperability with the NL-EUDI Wallet.

Successfully piloted with sports associations: verification drops from weeks to seconds, fraud is prevented by cryptographic signatures, admin burden disappears — and Justis has a clear path to large-scale digital issuance from 2026 onward.
useCases.userJourney:
1. A citizen needs a VOG for a job or volunteer role. The requesting organization initiates the VOG application, as in the existing process.

2. Justis performs the screening and, upon approval, issues the VOG as a cryptographically signed verifiable credential via Credenco's issuance platform (OpenID4VCI).

3. The citizen receives the VOG in their personal wallet (VOG app, interoperable with DIIP v5 and NL-EUDI wallets) and keeps full control over their data.

4. The citizen shares the VOG with the relying party (OpenID4VP): remotely via an emailed validation QR code/link, or in person via a QR scan at the point of entry.

5. The relying party (employer, sports club, school) verifies the credential in real time through the Credenco Business Wallet: Justis' signature, validity and revocation status are checked automatically.

6. Onboarding proceeds immediately — no paper, no manual checks. Verification drops from 1–7 weeks to seconds.

useCases.title: Preventing SIM Swap Fraud with EUDI Wallets and AI Voice Agents
useCases.summary:
Telcos handle some of the most sensitive account actions over the phone, especially SIM swaps, which are a primary vector for account takeover fraud. This usecase shows an AI voice agent that verifies a caller's identity against a digital wallet credential in real time, before any sensitive change is processed.

SIM swap fraud, phishing, and account takeover attacks all depend on the same weak point: phone-based identity checks that rely on security questions, personal data, or callback procedures, all of which can be socially engineered or leaked. Call center agents have no reliable way to confirm that the person on the line is who they claim to be, and attackers exploit exactly that gap.

For the telco, this closes the fraud gap without adding friction for legitimate customers. Verification happens automatically, mid-conversation, with no extra steps for the caller and no manual escalation for the agent. For the customer, it means sensitive requests are protected without the hassle of extra security questions or callback delays. For the industry more broadly, it demonstrates a reusable pattern for binding any high-risk transaction to a verified identity in real time.
useCases.userJourney:
1. Customer calls in. A customer contacts the telco to request a sensitive account change, for example a SIM swap.

2. AI voice agent picks up. The agent handles the call naturally, like a normal support conversation, and asks for the details of the request.

3. Identity binding happens mid-call. Before the agent proceeds, it binds the request to the customer's verified identity credential in real time. No security questions, no callback, no manual agent escalation.

4. Dashboard tracks the call live. A real-time dashboard shows each stage of the interaction as it happens: call received, identity check triggered, verification result, outcome.

5. Verification gates the outcome. If the identity check passes, the account change goes through. If it fails, the change is blocked on the spot, before any damage is done.

6.Loyalty credential issued. Once verified, the customer receives a loyalty credential as a reward for completing a secure interaction.

This flow removes the exact weak point that SIM swap attacks, phishing, and account takeover fraud rely on: social engineering and leaked personal data used to impersonate a real customer over the phone.

useCases.title: Buy Age-Restricted Goods Online in Seconds with EUDI Wallets
useCases.summary:
Buying age-restricted products online, like alcohol, still typically means uploading a passport scan and waiting for manual review, a slow and privacy-invasive process for both the customer and the retailer. This demo shows how an EUDI Wallet turns that into a checkout step that takes seconds, without disclosing any private information like date of birth.

Online retailers selling age-restricted goods have no fast, reliable way to confirm a buyer's age at checkout. Manual document review is slow, costly to operate, and requires customers to hand over far more personal data (full passport scans) than the transaction actually needs, just to prove one fact: that they are over 18.

For the retailer, age verification becomes instant and automated, removing manual review costs and reducing checkout drop-off. For the customer, there are no forms, no document uploads, and no waiting, just a quick scan and confirmation. For the ecosystem, it shows that minimal-disclosure verification (proving only "over 18" rather than full identity) is achievable today with wallets already in production, like France Identité.
useCases.userJourney:
1. Marie shops online. She adds gin and vodka, both age-restricted products, to her cart on an online store.

2. Checkout triggers age verification. At checkout, the store requests proof that Marie is over 18 before the order can proceed.

3. Marie scans a QR code. The store displays a QR code linked to the verification request.

4. Marie completes the check in her wallet app. She scans the code with her France Identité EUDI Wallet, reviews the request, and approves sharing only her age attribute.

5. Verification completes instantly. The wallet returns a verifiable proof of age to the retailer in real time.

6. Order is confirmed. With age confirmed, the order goes through immediately, no forms, no document upload, no manual review wait.

useCases.title: Verified machine safety access at Koning Willem I College (KW1C)
useCases.summary:
A student is trained on a high-risk workshop machine and receives a digital machine safety certificate. That same digital certificate lets the student book the machine online. Later, at the machine itself, the student holds their credential against the machine's reader. The same certificate is checked again, and only then does the physical lock release.

Most digital identity projects stay online: a credential is shown, a screen confirms it, done. This case bridges the online world and the physical world with the same credential and the same EUDI and ISO standards. Only the physical check of the certificate at the machine decides whether it runs at all. The machine either starts, or it stays locked.
useCases.userJourney:
A student completes safety training for a high-risk machine. KW1C, using its Sphereon VDX business wallet, issues a machine safety certificate as an ISO 18013-5 mdoc to the student's personal wallet.

To reserve a machine, the student logs in with their SURF eduID, which confirms they are enrolled at KW1C, and presents the safety certificate online. VDX verifies it, and only a valid certificate allows the student to make a reservation via the business wallet.

At the reserved time, the student stands at the machine and holds the same credential against the reader. VDX verifies it again, now in person over NFC/BLE. No person checks it; the machine does. 
On a successful check the existing Simac Pronto controller releases the physical lock. An unsuccessful check leaves the machine locked.

The innovation is the combination of digital and physical in one credential. The same certificate, issued once, is verified both ways: online when booking, and in person at the machine. Most digital identity stops at the screen. Here the digital reaches into the physical: it unlocks a real machine, or keeps it locked.

useCases.title: PASS2RENT: From Proof of Age to Open Door — Car Rental on EUDI Wallets
useCases.summary:
PASS2RENT demonstrates how EUDI Wallets can support an entire car-rental journey with privacy-preserving, interoperable credentials.

At booking, the driver proves the required age through the wallet. The rental platform receives only the driver's name and an age_over_18 result, not the birth date. At the vehicle, a mobile driving licence identifies the driver through a fresh, holder-bound presentation. No counter visit, photocopy or ID scan is required.

One in-house OpenID4VP verifier handles every interaction and accepted both France Identité and the European Commission's EUDI reference wallet without wallet-specific integration. Any birth date used to derive an age result is discarded within milliseconds and never reaches a database, API or webhook. The design also includes a tamper-evident audit trail with no personal data, encryption at rest, strict retention and erasure controls.

Demonstrated end to end, the use case shows that EUDI Wallets can replace document collection with selective disclosure and reusable, standards-based verification across different wallets and credential types.
useCases.userJourney:
https://api.playground.france-identite.gouv.fr/odifis/contactless-rent/en/

1. Booking. The driver selects a car and scans a QR code with France Identité. The rental platform receives only age_over_18: true. Any birth date disclosed to the verifier is discarded within milliseconds and never reaches the platform, its database or an API.

2. Identification. At the car, the driver presents a test mobile driving licence from the EU reference wallet, or uses the PID as a fallback. The same verifier checks the credential and shares only the structured claims needed for the rental—no scans or document images.

3. Handover. A fresh, device-bound presentation answers a dynamic challenge. After verification, the platform issues a short-lived, replay-protected token. Only a pseudonymous handover record and the verification method are retained.

4. Data minimisation. The database stores the age result, required rental claims and a pseudonymous attestation. It does not store a birth date, portrait, licence image or photocopy.

5. Trust. Credentials are checked against recognised trust anchors and revocation sources. Unknown issuers are flagged, never silently accepted.

useCases.title: Urban Company: Service Professional and Customer Identity Verification
useCases.summary:
Urban Company (Think Helpling, Taskrabbit, Bark etc) is one of Asia's leading technology platforms for 8.4 million users delivering home services, connecting customers with verified professionals across categories such as beauty, wellness, home cleaning, appliance repair, plumbing, electrical services, and home improvement.

Urban Company uses the Aadhaar App to enable secure, consent-based identity verification for both service professionals and customers. Service professionals can instantly verify their identity during onboarding, periodic re-verification, or before undertaking services at customer premises. Customers can also verify their identity, where required, for high-value or sensitive services. Using digitally signed verifiable credentials, the Aadhaar App enables users to share only the information necessary for the transaction, eliminating the need for physical identity documents. This reduces impersonation and fraud, streamlines onboarding and service delivery, enhances trust between professionals and customers, and provides a seamless, privacy-preserving verification experience.
useCases.userJourney:
### How It Works

1. A service professional begins onboarding through the Urban Company Partner App.

2. As part of the onboarding journey, the Partner App initiates an identity verification request by invoking the Aadhaar App.

3. The Aadhaar App opens and prompts the professional for consent to share the required identity information.

4. Upon consent, the Aadhaar App securely retrieves the required Aadhaar-based verifiable credential from the wallet and generates a digitally signed presentation containing only the requested demographic attributes.

5. The Aadhaar App returns the signed identity response directly to the Urban Company Partner App, which verifies the credential cryptographically using UIDAI's trust framework.

6. Once verification is successful, the professional's identity is confirmed instantly, allowing the onboarding process to continue without requiring physical documents, manual data entry, or document uploads.

This seamless app-to-app interaction enables secure, privacy-preserving, and paperless onboarding while significantly reducing onboarding time and the risk of document fraud or impersonation.

useCases.title: Hala Mobility: Verified Rider Onboarding
useCases.summary:
Hala Mobility is an electric mobility platform that manufactures and rents electric scooters to delivery partners, enabling last-mile logistics for food delivery, e-commerce, and quick commerce platforms. Similar to shared mobility providers such as Lime, Voi, and Tier in Europe, Hala Mobility enables riders to access vehicles without lengthy paperwork while ensuring a trusted onboarding process.

Before renting an electric scooter, Hala Mobility can use the Aadhaar App to perform secure, consent-based identity verification of delivery partners. Riders share a digitally signed verifiable credential from the Aadhaar App, allowing Hala Mobility to instantly verify their identity without requiring physical Aadhaar copies or manual document verification. This reduces onboarding time, prevents identity fraud, and enables a seamless, paperless rental experience while ensuring that only verified individuals are provided access to long-term vehicle rentals.
useCases.userJourney:
How It Works
A delivery partner applies to rent an electric scooter through the Hala Mobility application or onboarding portal.
During onboarding, Hala Mobility initiates an identity verification request by invoking the Aadhaar App.
The Aadhaar App opens and requests the rider's consent to share the required demographic information for identity verification.
Upon consent, the Aadhaar App generates a digitally signed verifiable credential containing only the requested identity attributes and securely shares it with the Hala Mobility application.
Hala Mobility verifies the credential cryptographically using UIDAI's trust framework, confirming that the identity information is authentic and has not been tampered with.
Once verification is successful, the rider's onboarding is completed, and the electric scooter can be rented to the verified individual for the agreed rental period.

This app-to-app verification flow enables fast, secure, and privacy-preserving rider onboarding while eliminating manual document verification and reducing the risk of identity fraud.

useCases.title: Tamil Nadu Medical Council: Doctor Identity Verification for Practitioner Registration

Applicants present their Aadhaar identity information through the Aadhaar App, allowing the Council to verify that the person applying is the legitimate holder of the identity and credentials submitted. This helps prevent impersonation or the misuse of another person's academic certificates to obtain a medical practitioner registration. Aadhaar verification forms one part of the Council's broader registration and credential verification process.
useCases.userJourney: An MBBS graduate applies for practitioner registration with the Tamil Nadu Medical Council. As part of the registration process, the applicant is asked to verify their identity using the Aadhaar App. The applicant presents their Aadhaar identity information and completes proof of presence through face verification. The Council verifies the presented identity and uses the verified information as part of its broader checks on the applicant's academic and professional credentials. Once the required checks are completed, the Council proceeds with the practitioner registration process.

useCases.title: Arattai: Verified Social Media Profiles
useCases.summary:
Arattai is an Indian instant messaging and social networking platform (Like WhatsApp and Signal) with 8 million users that enables users to connect, communicate, and build trusted online communities. By integrating with the Aadhaar App, Arattai can offer users the option to verify their identity and receive a Verified Profile badge.

Users can securely share a digitally signed verifiable credential from the Aadhaar App with their explicit consent, allowing Arattai to confirm that the profile belongs to a real individual without storing or exposing unnecessary personal information. This helps reduce fake accounts, impersonation, bots, and identity fraud while enabling users to build credibility and trust on the platform. The verification is privacy-preserving, paperless, and based on cryptographically verifiable digital credentials, giving users greater control over their identity while fostering a safer and more authentic social media experience.
useCases.userJourney:
A user downloads Arattai, creates a profile, and can immediately access the platform's messaging and social features without completing identity verification.

If the user chooses to verify their profile, Arattai initiates an app-to-app verification request to the Aadhaar App or another compatible digital identity wallet, such as Google Wallet. The user reviews the identity request and provides consent to share the required credential.

The wallet presents a verifiable identity credential to Arattai. Arattai cryptographically verifies the credential and, once verification is successful, updates the user's profile to display a verified status.

Other users can then see that the profile has been verified using a trusted digital identity credential. The verification provides an additional layer of assurance without requiring Arattai to collect or store copies of the user's identity document.

useCases.title: Swiggy: Delivery Agent and Customer Identity Verification

Swiggy (Think Ubereats, Just Eat, Wolt for an european comparison) is one of India's largest on-demand convenience platforms, serving 120 million customers across hundreds of cities through its food delivery, quick commerce, grocery, and logistics services.

Swiggy uses the Aadhaar App to enable secure, consent-based identity verification for both delivery partners and customers. Delivery agents can instantly prove their identity during onboarding, periodic re-verification, or when collecting high-value or age-restricted orders. Similarly, customers can verify their identity, where required, before receiving sensitive deliveries. The Aadhaar App allows users to share only the necessary information through digitally signed verifiable credentials, eliminating the need for physical documents or photocopies. useCases.userJourney:

For regular deliveries, no additional identity verification is required. For restricted-item deliveries, the delivery partner and recipient can mutually verify each other using the Aadhaar App or any compatible digital identity wallet. The recipient can verify the assigned delivery partner, while the delivery partner can verify the required identity or eligibility attributes of the recipient before completing the delivery.

useCases.title: Spherity’s Digital Product Passports for BVG’s Electric Bus Batteries
useCases.summary: BVG, Berlin’s public transport operator, uses Spherity’s Digital Product Passport solution for batteries installed in its electric bus fleet. Each battery is connected to a digital passport containing standardized information on its composition, material sourcing, carbon footprint, regulatory documentation, performance, and lifecycle. The implementation supports transparent, machine-readable compliance reporting and gives BVG access to up-to-date information on battery health and environmental impact. The first buses equipped with these digital battery passports entered operation in December 2024, helping BVG prepare for the requirements of the EU Battery Regulation ahead of the 2027 deadline.
useCases.userJourney: Battery and product data from the vehicle manufacturer and relevant technical systems is connected to Spherity’s DPP software. A unique digital passport is created for each battery unit and linked to the physical battery through a product identifier and QR code. The solution structures and validates information such as battery composition, sourcing, carbon footprint, regulatory documents, and operational performance. BVG can access this information during the battery’s use phase for compliance reporting, sustainability assessment, maintenance, and lifecycle management, while other authorised parties may provide or retrieve information relevant to their role. The passport can be updated as the battery is operated, serviced, reused, or recycled, creating a continuous and trusted record across its lifecycle.

useCases.title: Faydapass
useCases.summary: FaydaPass solves Ethiopia's fragmented, paper-based identity problem, where citizens repeatedly re-prove who they are to disconnected institutions, leaving services slow, exclusionary, and open to fraud and duplicate benefit claims. It creates value by letting NIDP anchor a trusted "Fayda Credential" from which institutions like Ministry of Education, Ethiopia Food and Drug Authority, banks, and Ministry of Health can issue and verify their own credentials giving citizens faster, safer access; institutions instant verification; and government a way to cut fraud and advance Digital Ethiopia 2030. The key roles are the Issuer (grants a credential), the Holder (the citizen or guardian), and the Verifier (checks a credential)  with the digital wallet as the citizen's interface for selectively sharing credentials, online or offline, and Verifiable Credentials as the tamper-proof proof objects that let any verifier trust a claim instantly, without contacting the original issuer.
useCases.userJourney: NIDP enrolls the citizen once, outside the wallet, issuing their Fayda ID. The citizen installs FaydaPass and authenticates via eSignet (Fayda ID + OTP/biometric); the wallet requests the Fayda Credential (Anchor) over OpenID4VCI, and NIDP issues it bound to the device key, establishing the wallet's root of trust and enabling login/TOTP. Sector institutions (MoE, EFDA, MoH, Civil Service Commission, MoA/ATI, NBE) issue credentials on top of the anchor when the citizen requests them, resolving identity against the Fayda ID each time; issuance is citizen-initiated, issuer-authorized. At service points, the citizen scans the relying party's QR, reviews requested attributes, and consents to share only those  license validity without the registration number, online or offline. The verifier checks the signature, issuer trust, and holder binding without contacting the issuer, confirming revocation via a status endpoint or cached list offline. useCases.title: Tax Splitter: real-time VAT collection with verifiable organisational identity
useCases.summary:
The European Commission estimates the annual EU VAT gap at EUR 128 billion (2023). At the same time, Dutch entrepreneurs spend 30 to 40 hours per year on VAT administration. Both problems share a root cause: tax compliance happens after the fact, through declarations, reconciliation and audits.

Tax Splitter turns that around. Every transaction automatically splits the VAT amount and transfers it directly to the tax authority at the moment of payment. A business owner no longer needs to reserve, calculate or declare VAT. The invoice is the return.

The mechanism is digital trust. Organisations hold verifiable credentials (issued by Credenco) in organisational wallets, so every payment starts with an identity lookup: is the counterparty a real, registered business or a shell company? The payment itself carries a cryptographic reference to the invoice, creating an audit trail that all parties can verify without exposing the underlying data: proofs are shared, not the records themselves. Each party keeps control of its own data; the infrastructure moves sealed envelopes, it never looks inside. Parties that don't share databases share cryptographic proof instead.

The system was developed over two years by the Dutch Tax Authority (Directorate Control and Finance, problem owner), mintBlue (infrastructure and development) and Credenco (verifiable credentials and digital identity), through a Design Sprint and two completed development phases. It runs as a proof of concept with a working end-to-end demonstration: visitors buy a product at a point-of-sale system, pay with a wallet, and watch the VAT split and settle in real-time. A pilot with real entrepreneurs is in preparation, and the tax authority has driven the project itself at every step, from the design sprint to the working demonstration.

In March 2026, Tax Splitter won the Innovation Award of the Dutch Ministry of Finance. The OECD cites the project in its Tax Administration Series as an inspiring example of real-time tax collection. Where the EU's ViDA legislation (VAT in the Digital Age) introduces real-time reporting from 2028, Tax Splitter goes one step further and collects the tax as the payment happens.

The same pattern applies to any predictable levy. The partners are exploring gambling tax, property transfer tax, excise duties, tourist levies and cross-border VAT, where the tax automatically reaches the tax authority of the right country. The approach is drawing interest from tax authorities in the United Kingdom and Scandinavia.
useCases.userJourney:
1. In the proof of concept, a seller issues an invoice. Before any money moves, the buyer's system performs an identity lookup on the seller's verifiable organisational credential, issued by Credenco. The check rejects shell companies before the payment can start.

2. The buyer pays from an organisational wallet, at a point-of-sale terminal or online. The wallet holds the organisation's credentials, so every payment is bound to a verified legal identity.

3. At the moment of payment the amount splits automatically: the net amount settles with the seller, the VAT portion transfers directly to the tax authority's wallet. No one has to set money aside or file anything.

4. The payment carries a cryptographic reference to the underlying invoice. Invoice and payment are verifiably linked in a single audit trail that all parties can check without exposing the underlying business data to anyone else.

5. The tax authority follows VAT flows in real-time through its portal and handles settlement and refunds over the same infrastructure. Discrepancies surface immediately instead of months after a quarterly declaration.

6. The entrepreneur does nothing: no reserving, no calculating, no declaring. The invoice is the return.

The demonstration is a simplified consumer version of this business-to-business flow: at a physical point-of-sale setup, visitors buy a product, pay with a demonstration wallet, and see the VAT reach the tax authority's wallet on the spot.

useCases.title: Municipal login with attribute-based credentials
useCases.summary: Citizens log in to their municipal account and securely share only the personal attributes a service actually needs, using an attribute-based wallet. The municipality acts as the relying party and verifies the presented attributes over the IRMA protocol. This is one of the first production implementations of attribute-based authentication in Dutch municipal services, showing that privacy-friendly login at scale is possible today.
useCases.userJourney:
1) The citizen has loaded personal attributes (e.g. name, email, mobile number) into an attribute-based wallet.
2) They open their municipal account and choose to log in with the wallet.
3) The municipality (relying party) requests only the attributes required for the service over the IRMA protocol.
4) The citizen reviews the request in the wallet and confirms disclosure.
5) The municipality verifies the attributes and grants access, without storing more personal data than necessary.

useCases.title: Age verification for online purchases
useCases.summary: An online shop confirms a customer is old enough to buy an age-restricted product before it can be added to the cart, without learning their date of birth or identity. The shop acts as the relying party and requests a simple over-18 proof from the customer's wallet over OpenID4VP. Because only the age attribute is disclosed, the flow is privacy-friendly by design and removes the friction of uploading ID documents during checkout.
useCases.userJourney:
1) The customer adds an age-restricted product to their basket in the web shop.
2) Before checkout, the shop (relying party) requests proof that the customer is over the required age.
3) The wallet presents only an over-18 attribute over OpenID4VP — no date of birth, no full identity.
4) The shop verifies the proof and unlocks the purchase.
5) The customer completes checkout without uploading ID documents or sharing unnecessary personal data.

useCases.title: Digital travel credential at check-in and boarding
useCases.summary: Travellers move through check-in and boarding by presenting credentials from their wallet at a proximity touchpoint, instead of juggling paper documents. The airline acts as the relying party and verifies an ISO-based digital identity (Photo ID / mDL) together with IATA travel credentials such as a boarding pass and booking order. The same pattern is being demonstrated by multiple airlines and airports (e.g. Air New Zealand, British Airways, Japan Airlines, IndiGo, Hong Kong and Bengaluru airports), pointing to an interoperable, document-light travel journey.
useCases.userJourney:
1) The traveller holds a Photo ID / mDL and IATA travel credentials (boarding pass, booking order) in a supported wallet.
2) At check-in or the boarding gate, a proximity reader requests the relevant credentials.
3) The wallet shows the request; the traveller approves the presentation by tapping or scanning.
4) The airline (relying party) verifies the digital identity and travel documents over an ISO/IEC 18013-5 flow.
5) The traveller proceeds without presenting paper documents, sharing only what is needed for that step.
